negotiation_game.title: Negotiation Arena
negotiation_game.description: Practice real-world negotiation skills in guided scenarios with AI characters.

help_content.what_is: Negotiation is the art of finding solutions that work for everyone. In these scenarios, you'll practice persuading, compromising, and creating win-win outcomes.
tips: Try to understand the other person's needs
Know your BATNA (Best Alternative) before you start

scenarios.title: Study Group Scheduling
scenarios.description: Your classmate Arjun wants to schedule a study group meeting, but the proposed time clashes with your cricket practice. Find a time that works for both of you.
scenarios.cultural_context: Indian school setting where balancing academics with sports is important. Respect for each other's commitments matters.
scenarios.your_objective: Find a study group time that doesn't conflict with your cricket practice (Mon/Wed/Fri 4-6 PM). You need to study for the upcoming math exam.
scenarios.your_batna: Study alone using online resources, but you'll miss out on group problem-solving which helps you understand better.

other_party.name: Arjun
other_party.personality: Organized and slightly stubborn, but reasonable when given good reasons. Values academics highly.
other_party.objective: Schedule the study group at a time when most members can attend. Arjun prefers weekday afternoons.
other_party.batna: Hold the study group without you, but the group works best with everyone present.
other_party.cultural_notes: Arjun respects people who are direct but polite. He responds well to logical arguments.
other_party.conversation_style: Direct and practical, uses facts to support his position

scoring_criteria.relationship: Did you maintain a good relationship with Arjun?
scoring_criteria.win_win: Did you find a solution that works for both of you?
scoring_criteria.communication: Were you clear and respectful in your communication?
scoring_criteria.batna_usage: Did you use your alternatives strategically?

coaching_tips: Start by acknowledging Arjun's effort in organizing the study group
Share your schedule constraint clearly — don't hide it
Suggest alternative times instead of just saying 'no'
Ask Arjun what times work for other members too
learning_objectives: Practice assertive communication
Learn to propose alternatives, not just reject ideas
Build collaborative problem-solving skills

storybook_pages.title: The Scheduling Conflict
storybook_pages.text: Lunch break at your school canteen. Arjun has just posted in the class WhatsApp group — 'Study group for math exam, Monday 4 PM at my house.' Your heart sinks. That's exactly when cricket practice starts.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian school canteen with students eating lunch, one student looking at phone with worried expression, colorful tiffin boxes on table, warm school setting, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: What's at Stake
storybook_pages.text: Cricket selections are next month — you can't miss practice. But the math exam? You barely passed the last unit test. The study group is your best shot at understanding calculus. You need both.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Split scene showing cricket ground with players practicing on left and math textbooks with calculus equations on right, Indian teenage student in the middle looking torn between both, warm colors, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Time to Negotiate
storybook_pages.text: You spot Arjun at the canteen counter. He's organizing everything — notes, venue, snacks. This is your chance. How will you convince him to shift the timing without seeming difficult?
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Two Indian teenage boys at school canteen, one holding a notebook with plans and looking organized, the other approaching with a friendly but determined smile, warm school atmosphere, illustration style

scenarios.title: The Pocket Money Talk
scenarios.description: You want to convince your parent to increase your monthly pocket money. You need to make a compelling case while being respectful.
scenarios.cultural_context: Indian family where parents are respected but also open to reasonable discussions. Money conversations require sensitivity and maturity.
scenarios.your_objective: Get your pocket money increased from Rs 500 to Rs 800 per month. You have genuine expenses — school supplies, occasional outings with friends, and saving for a book you want.
scenarios.your_batna: Keep current pocket money and find small ways to earn extra (helping neighbors, selling old books). Not ideal but manageable.

other_party.name: Amma
other_party.occupation: Your parent (works as a school teacher)
other_party.personality: Caring but financially careful. Values responsibility and maturity in children. Impressed by good reasoning rather than emotional arguments.
other_party.objective: Keep household expenses manageable. Wants to see that the child is responsible with money before increasing allowance.
other_party.batna: Offer to increase pocket money slightly (Rs 100) or offer to cover specific expenses directly rather than giving cash.
other_party.cultural_notes: Responds well to respectful tone. Dislikes comparison with other families. Values when children show they understand the family's financial situation.
other_party.conversation_style: Warm but practical, asks probing questions, appreciates honesty

scoring_criteria.relationship: Did you maintain respect and warmth in the conversation?
scoring_criteria.win_win: Did you find a solution that addresses both your needs and your parent's concerns?
scoring_criteria.communication: Were you clear, mature, and persuasive?
scoring_criteria.batna_usage: Did you show awareness of alternatives?

coaching_tips: Show you understand the family budget is limited
Present specific expenses — vague requests are weak
Offer to take on responsibilities in return
Be willing to accept a compromise
learning_objectives: Practice persuasion with authority figures
Learn to build a case with evidence
Develop empathy for the other side's constraints

storybook_pages.title: The Monthly Squeeze
storybook_pages.text: It's the 20th of the month and your wallet is empty again. Rs 500 just doesn't stretch — between notebook refills, bus fare for the school trip, and that one outing with friends, the money vanishes before the month ends.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian teenager sitting at desk counting coins from a small wallet, empty piggy bank nearby, school supplies and a wish-list notebook visible, cozy bedroom setting, warm lighting, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Building Your Case
storybook_pages.text: You grab a notebook and start listing your expenses. School supplies: Rs 200. Transport: Rs 150. One outing: Rs 200. That's already Rs 550 for basics alone. You need facts, not feelings, for this conversation.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Close-up of a handwritten expense list in a notebook with Indian rupee amounts, calculator and pen beside it, student's hand writing carefully, organized and determined mood, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The After-Dinner Talk
storybook_pages.text: Dinner is over. Amma is reading the newspaper in the living room. The TV is off — perfect timing. You take a deep breath. This isn't about demanding more money. It's about showing you're responsible enough to handle it.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Warm Indian living room after dinner, mother reading newspaper on sofa, teenager standing at doorway looking thoughtful and preparing to speak, traditional home decor, evening lighting, illustration style

scenarios.title: The Group Project Debate
scenarios.description: Your school group project needs a leader, and both you and your friend Meera want to lead the presentation. Negotiate roles that play to everyone's strengths.
scenarios.cultural_context: Indian school setting where group harmony matters but individual contributions are also valued. The teacher will evaluate both teamwork and the quality of the final presentation.
scenarios.your_objective: Get the lead presenter role because you've been practicing public speaking. You're also okay with co-leading if Meera handles the research since she's better at that.
scenarios.your_batna: Take the research lead role instead — still a strong contribution, but you'd miss the speaking practice you want.

other_party.name: Meera
other_party.personality: Creative and detail-oriented. Can be competitive but ultimately values friendship. Wants recognition for her contributions.
other_party.objective: Lead the presentation because she designed the slides and feels ownership of the content. Also wants to build her confidence in public speaking.
other_party.batna: Co-present with someone else, or take full credit for the visual design aspect.
other_party.cultural_notes: Meera values fairness and reciprocity. She'll compromise if she feels her contributions are acknowledged.
other_party.conversation_style: Expressive and passionate, can get defensive if she feels dismissed

scoring_criteria.relationship: Did you preserve your friendship with Meera?
scoring_criteria.win_win: Did you find a creative role assignment that works for both?

coaching_tips: Acknowledge Meera's hard work on the slides first
Share why the presenting role matters to you — be honest
Explore splitting the presentation into sections
Think about what each of you is best at
learning_objectives: Practice creative problem-solving in conflicts
Learn to acknowledge others' contributions
Develop skills in collaborative role negotiation

storybook_pages.title: The Group Project Dilemma
storybook_pages.text: Mrs. Sharma just announced the final project — a 15-minute presentation worth 30% of your grade. 'Choose your team roles wisely,' she says. You and Meera exchange a glance. You both want to lead.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian school classroom, teacher at blackboard writing 'Final Project - 30%', two students in the class exchanging a competitive but friendly glance, other students around them, school setting, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Meera's Perspective
storybook_pages.text: You pass the computer lab and spot Meera still there at 6 PM. She's been working on the slides for hours — beautiful charts, custom animations, original artwork. She clearly cares deeply about this project.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian teenage girl working late at school computer lab, creating beautiful presentation slides with charts and animations on screen, determined expression, evening light through windows, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Library Meeting
storybook_pages.text: After school, you walk into the library study room. Meera is already there, notes spread across the table. She looks up. 'So... about who's presenting.' The tension is real, but so is the friendship.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: School library study room with books on shelves, two Indian teenagers sitting across a table with notes spread out, one looking determined the other thoughtful, afternoon light, illustration style

scenarios.title: The Street Market Deal
scenarios.description: You're at a local market in Pune trying to buy a cricket bat for your school tournament. The shopkeeper quotes a high price. Negotiate a fair deal.
scenarios.setting: Laxmi Road sports goods market, Pune
scenarios.cultural_context: Indian street market culture where bargaining is expected and even enjoyed. The shopkeeper respects smart buyers who negotiate well. Being too aggressive or too passive both lead to bad deals.
scenarios.your_objective: Buy a good quality cricket bat within your budget of Rs 1200. The shopkeeper is asking Rs 1800. You've seen similar bats online for Rs 1300-1400.
scenarios.your_batna: Buy online for Rs 1350 (but delivery takes a week and you can't test the bat). Or check the next shop.

other_party.name: Sharma Uncle
other_party.personality: Experienced negotiator, friendly but shrewd. Enjoys the bargaining process. Gives better deals to customers he likes.
other_party.objective: Sell the bat at Rs 1500 or above for a good profit margin. Cost price is Rs 1000.
other_party.batna: Sell to another customer — tournament season means high demand. He can easily sell at Rs 1600 to someone less careful.
other_party.cultural_notes: Responds well to charm and humor. Dislikes customers who are rude or who lowball immediately. Offers chai to serious buyers.
other_party.conversation_style: Animated, tells stories, uses humor, drops hints about 'special price for you'

scoring_criteria.relationship: Did you build rapport with the shopkeeper?
scoring_criteria.win_win: Did you get a fair price that both sides are happy with?
scoring_criteria.batna_usage: Did you use market research and alternatives effectively?

coaching_tips: Start with friendly conversation — ask about his shop, the tournament season
Inspect the bat carefully — show you know quality
Mention what you've seen online but don't threaten to leave immediately
Start your counter-offer at Rs 1000 to leave room for negotiation
If stuck, ask about bundle deals (bat + grip + ball)
learning_objectives: Practice market bargaining in a culturally appropriate way
Learn anchoring and counter-anchoring techniques
Develop confidence in transactional negotiations

storybook_pages.title: Tournament Season
storybook_pages.text: The school notice board says it all — Inter-School Cricket Tournament, two weeks away. Your old bat has a crack running down the blade. You need a new one, and it has to be good. Dad gave you Rs 1200 and said 'Make it count.'
storybook_pages.image_prompt: School notice board with cricket tournament poster, Indian teenager looking at it with excitement and determination, cricket bat with a visible crack leaning against the wall nearby, school corridor, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Laxmi Road Market
storybook_pages.text: The famous Laxmi Road sports market is buzzing. Shops lined up with bats, pads, and gloves hanging from every corner. The smell of leather and willow fills the air. Sharma Uncle's shop catches your eye — 'Champion Sports, Since 1998.'
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Bustling Indian street market in Pune with sports equipment shops, cricket bats and pads displayed, colorful signboards, crowds of shoppers, a prominent shop with 'Champion Sports' sign, vibrant market scene, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Shopkeeper's Quote
storybook_pages.text: 'This one? Ah, excellent choice beta!' Sharma Uncle pulls out a gleaming English willow bat. 'For you, special price — only Rs 1800.' Your budget is Rs 1200. Online it's Rs 1350. The negotiation begins.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian sports shop interior, friendly middle-aged shopkeeper holding up a cricket bat proudly, young customer looking at price tag with slight concern, bats and equipment on display walls, warm shop lighting, illustration style

scenarios.title: The Internship Opportunity
scenarios.description: A startup founder visits your college for a guest lecture. After the talk, you have a chance to pitch yourself for a summer internship. Make it count.
scenarios.setting: College auditorium lobby after a guest lecture
scenarios.cultural_context: Indian college setting where internships are highly competitive. First impressions matter. The founder values initiative and genuine interest over polished resumes.
scenarios.your_objective: Convince Vikram to give you a summer internship at his ed-tech startup. You don't have much experience, but you're eager to learn and have relevant project work to show.
scenarios.your_batna: Apply through the college placement cell for other internships, or do a self-guided project over summer. Less exciting but still productive.

other_party.name: Vikram
other_party.occupation: Founder of a growing ed-tech startup, IIT alumnus
other_party.personality: Energetic, values hustle and genuine curiosity. Hates scripted pitches. Looks for raw talent and authentic passion over credentials.
other_party.objective: Find an intern who can genuinely contribute — someone self-motivated who won't need constant hand-holding. Has limited budget for interns.
other_party.batna: Hire through LinkedIn or get referrals from IIT network. Doesn't need to fill the position today.
other_party.cultural_notes: Vikram respects students who do their homework about his company. He's turned off by name-dropping or grade-boasting.
other_party.conversation_style: Casual but sharp, asks unexpected questions, values authenticity

scoring_criteria.relationship: Did you build genuine rapport with Vikram?
scoring_criteria.win_win: Did you show how you'd add value (not just what you'd gain)?
scoring_criteria.communication: Were you authentic, concise, and confident?
scoring_criteria.batna_usage: Did you show initiative beyond just wanting the internship?

coaching_tips: Research his startup before approaching — mention something specific you admire
Lead with what you can contribute, not what you want to learn
Be honest about your skill level — founders respect self-awareness
Have a specific project idea that could help his startup
Ask a thoughtful question about his company's challenges
learning_objectives: Practice self-marketing in professional settings
Learn to build quick rapport with senior professionals
Develop a clear personal value proposition

storybook_pages.title: The Guest Lecture
storybook_pages.text: Vikram Rao just delivered a fire talk on 'Building Products That Matter.' The auditorium is buzzing. He founded EduSpark — an ed-tech startup that's been in the news. And he just mentioned they're looking for summer interns.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian college auditorium with a young startup founder on stage giving an inspiring talk, students in audience taking notes excitedly, 'Building Products That Matter' on the screen behind, energetic atmosphere, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Your Chance
storybook_pages.text: The lecture ends. Students swarm Vikram for selfies. But you notice — he looks bored by the crowd. He's packing up his laptop. If you want to stand out, you need more than 'Sir, can I get an internship?' You need a real pitch.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: College auditorium lobby, startup founder surrounded by students taking selfies, one student standing slightly apart looking thoughtful and preparing mentally, contrast between crowd and focused individual, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Five Minutes to Shine
storybook_pages.text: The crowd thins. Vikram heads for the exit. You fall into step beside him. 'Vikram sir, I have an idea for your Tier-2 city expansion...' He pauses. Turns. 'I'm listening.' This is your moment.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: College corridor, young Indian startup founder pausing mid-walk to listen to a confident student, both walking side by side, the student gesturing while explaining an idea, hopeful determined expression, illustration style

scenarios.title: The Campus Interview
scenarios.description: You've cleared the aptitude test and group discussion for a startup during campus placement. Now comes the HR interview — where you negotiate your role, start date, and work arrangements.
scenarios.cultural_context: Indian campus placement where students often accept the first offer without negotiating. Companies expect some back-and-forth. Standing your ground politely shows maturity.
scenarios.your_objective: Secure a role in product development (not customer support, which they might push you towards). Negotiate a July start date (not June, as you have a family wedding). Also explore remote work options for the first month.
scenarios.your_batna: You have another offer from a mid-size IT company — stable but less exciting. You prefer the startup for learning opportunities.

other_party.name: Priya Ma'am
other_party.occupation: HR Manager at GrowthBox (a SaaS startup)
other_party.personality: Professional, warm but firm on company needs. Values candidates who know what they want. Secretly admires negotiators — sees it as a sign of leadership.
other_party.objective: Fill the customer success role first (it's urgent). Wants June joiners. Flexible on remote work if the candidate is strong.
other_party.batna: Five other shortlisted candidates willing to accept any role and start date.
other_party.cultural_notes: Priya respects directness but expects politeness. She sees negotiation as a positive signal. She dislikes indecisiveness.
other_party.conversation_style: Structured and professional, probes motivations, gives hints about flexibility

scoring_criteria.relationship: Did you maintain a professional and warm dynamic with Priya?
scoring_criteria.win_win: Did you secure terms that work for both you and the company?
scoring_criteria.communication: Were you clear about your preferences without being rigid?
scoring_criteria.batna_usage: Did you leverage your alternative offer strategically?

coaching_tips: Express genuine interest in the company before negotiating terms
Explain WHY you prefer product development — link it to your skills
Mention your other offer subtly, not as a threat
Be flexible on one point to gain on another
Ask questions that show you've researched the company
learning_objectives: Practice professional negotiation in interview settings
Learn to articulate career preferences confidently
Develop skills in balancing assertiveness with flexibility

storybook_pages.title: Placement Season
storybook_pages.text: The placement cell is electric. GrowthBox — the hottest SaaS startup in Bangalore — is on campus today. You cleared the aptitude test. Smashed the group discussion. Now there's one final round: the HR interview with Priya Ma'am.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian college placement cell with students in formal wear waiting nervously, a startup company banner 'GrowthBox' on the wall, one confident student walking towards the interview room, campus placement season atmosphere, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: What You Want vs What They Need
storybook_pages.text: You've done your research. GrowthBox needs customer success hires urgently, but their product team is where the real growth is. You want product development. They want you to start in June. You need July. This won't be a simple 'yes sir.'
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Split scene showing a startup office with product development team on one side and customer support team on other side, Indian student in center comparing both options, thought bubble with calendar showing June vs July, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Interview Room
storybook_pages.text: Room 104. Priya Ma'am smiles warmly. 'Congratulations on making it this far. So, tell me — what role do you see yourself in at GrowthBox?' This is it. The negotiation starts with your very first answer.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Professional interview room in Indian college, HR manager woman sitting across table smiling warmly, nervous but prepared student sitting opposite with notes, company logo on the wall, professional setting, illustration style

scenarios.title: The First Salary Talk
scenarios.description: You've received a job offer, but the salary is Rs 4.5 LPA — below the market rate of Rs 5.5-6 LPA for your role. Time to negotiate your worth.
scenarios.setting: Video call with the company's HR recruiter
scenarios.cultural_context: Indian job market where salary negotiation is uncommon among fresh graduates, but increasingly valued. Many candidates accept the first number out of fear. Companies often have room to negotiate.
scenarios.your_objective: Negotiate your CTC from Rs 4.5 LPA to at least Rs 5.5 LPA, or get meaningful perks — joining bonus, early review cycle, or higher variable pay. Don't lose the offer.
scenarios.your_batna: You have a competing offer at Rs 5 LPA from another company, but the role is less interesting. You could also freelance while searching for better opportunities.

other_party.name: Rahul
other_party.occupation: Senior HR recruiter at a mid-size tech company
other_party.personality: Friendly but follows company guidelines. Has a salary band he can't exceed easily. Respects data-driven arguments. Can offer non-salary perks more easily than base salary bumps.
other_party.objective: Close the offer within the approved salary band (Rs 4.2-5.8 LPA). Wants to fill the position quickly. Prefers candidates who don't play hardball.
other_party.batna: Two other candidates in the pipeline. One accepted at Rs 4.5 LPA already.
other_party.cultural_notes: Rahul values professionalism. He's put off by entitlement but impressed by market research. He has more flexibility on perks than base salary.
other_party.conversation_style: Professional, occasionally drops hints about flexibility, responds to data

scoring_criteria.relationship: Did you maintain a positive relationship throughout?
scoring_criteria.win_win: Did you achieve a better package while keeping the recruiter satisfied?
scoring_criteria.communication: Were you data-driven, confident, and professional?
scoring_criteria.batna_usage: Did you use your competing offer and market data strategically?

coaching_tips: Start by expressing genuine excitement about the role
Present market salary data from Glassdoor, AmbitionBox, LinkedIn
Never give an ultimatum — keep the door open
If base salary is stuck, negotiate perks: joining bonus, WFH, early appraisal
Practice saying the number you want out loud before the call
learning_objectives: Learn to research and present market compensation data
Practice assertive salary negotiation as a fresh graduate
Develop confidence in knowing and stating your worth

storybook_pages.title: The Offer Letter
storybook_pages.text: The email lands at 9 AM. 'Congratulations! We're pleased to offer you the role of Software Developer at Rs 4.5 LPA.' Your heart races — you got the job! But then you check Glassdoor. The market rate for this role is Rs 5.5-6 LPA.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian young professional looking at laptop screen showing an offer letter email, mixed emotions of excitement and concern, salary figures visible, Glassdoor tab open on another screen showing higher market rates, home desk setup, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Doing Your Homework
storybook_pages.text: You spend the evening researching. AmbitionBox says Rs 5.2 LPA average. LinkedIn shows similar roles at Rs 5.5-6 LPA. Your college's placement data confirms it. You're being lowballed — but you also really want this role.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian student at desk late evening with multiple browser tabs open showing salary data, charts and graphs on screen, notebook with comparisons written down, determined focused expression, warm desk lamp lighting, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Call
storybook_pages.text: Rahul from HR calls: 'Hey, did you get the offer? Any questions?' This is your window. You have the data. You have a competing offer. You have 10 minutes to change your starting salary. Deep breath.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian young professional on video call with HR recruiter, laptop screen showing the call, notepad with talking points ready, phone showing competing offer email, moment of truth expression, professional home setup, illustration style

scenarios.title: The Scholarship Plea
scenarios.description: You've been accepted to your dream college, but the fees are steep. You're meeting the Admissions Head to discuss scholarship options and financial aid.
scenarios.setting: Admissions office of a prestigious private college
scenarios.cultural_context: Indian higher education where private college fees can be a major burden. Scholarships often exist but aren't widely advertised. Showing merit, financial need, and genuine passion can unlock hidden opportunities.
scenarios.your_objective: Secure at least a 40% fee reduction through scholarship, merit award, or work-study arrangement. The annual fee is Rs 3 lakhs. Your family can afford Rs 1.8 lakhs maximum.
scenarios.your_batna: Got admission to a government college with low fees but less prestige and fewer opportunities. Could also take an education loan, but that means starting career with debt.

other_party.name: Dr. Nair
other_party.occupation: Head of Admissions at Prestige Institute
other_party.personality: Experienced administrator who genuinely cares about students but must balance budgets. Has seen thousands of scholarship requests. Values authentic stories over sob stories.
other_party.objective: Fill the class with talented students while maintaining financial sustainability. Has a limited scholarship fund. Prefers to give partial scholarships to more students than full scholarships to few.
other_party.batna: Hundreds of applicants willing to pay full fees. The college doesn't need to offer discounts.
other_party.cultural_notes: Dr. Nair respects students who show they've explored all options. He values future potential as much as past achievements.
other_party.conversation_style: Kind but businesslike, asks pointed questions, appreciates preparation

scoring_criteria.relationship: Did you build a respectful rapport with Dr. Nair?
scoring_criteria.win_win: Did you find a financial arrangement that works for both sides?
scoring_criteria.communication: Were you honest, prepared, and persuasive?
scoring_criteria.batna_usage: Did you mention alternatives without sounding like you're threatening to leave?

coaching_tips: Lead with your achievements and potential, not just financial need
Have specific numbers ready — your family income, expenses, gap amount
Ask about ALL options: merit scholarship, need-based aid, work-study, installment plans
Show you've researched the college thoroughly — mention specific programs you're excited about
Be willing to take a partial scholarship plus other arrangements
learning_objectives: Practice persuading authority figures with preparation and authenticity
Learn to present financial situations professionally
Develop creative problem-solving for financial negotiations

storybook_pages.title: The Dream Acceptance
storybook_pages.text: The acceptance email from Prestige Institute glows on your screen. You made it! Top 5% nationally. But then you scroll to the fee structure: Rs 3,00,000 per year. Your family earns Rs 6 lakhs. The dream suddenly feels impossibly expensive.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian student reading college acceptance email on phone with a huge smile that slowly fades, fee structure document visible, family photos in background of a modest home, mixed emotions of joy and worry, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Family Discussion
storybook_pages.text: At dinner, Dad says, 'We'll manage somehow.' But you see Amma doing mental math, worry creasing her face. You overhear them talking about selling the scooter. No — you won't let them sacrifice that much. There must be another way.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian family at dinner table having a serious discussion, father looking supportive, mother doing calculations on phone, teenager looking determined and thoughtful, modest but warm Indian dining room, evening setting, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Admissions Office
storybook_pages.text: Prestige Institute's campus is stunning — manicured lawns, modern labs, students buzzing with energy. You're in the admissions waiting room, portfolio in hand. Dr. Nair will see you in five minutes. You've prepared your case. Time to make it count.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Beautiful Indian private college campus with modern buildings and green lawns, young student sitting in admissions office waiting room holding a folder, looking determined and well-prepared, prestigious academic setting, illustration style

scenarios.title: The Roommate Conflict
scenarios.description: Your college hostel roommate Karthik has been playing loud music late at night before your important exam. Tensions are rising. Time to resolve this before the friendship — and your grades — suffer.
scenarios.cultural_context: Indian college hostel life where sharing small rooms requires constant adjustment. Direct confrontation is uncomfortable but necessary. Passive aggression makes things worse. The warden getting involved means trouble for both.
scenarios.your_objective: Get Karthik to keep quiet after 11 PM on weeknights, especially during exam week. Maintain the friendship — you have to live together for 8 more months. Find a solution you both can live with.
scenarios.your_batna: Complain to the hostel warden (but this damages the friendship and makes you 'that person'). Or study in the library (but it closes at 10 PM). Or use earplugs (but they're uncomfortable and you can't hear your alarm).

other_party.name: Karthik
other_party.personality: Friendly and social but inconsiderate of others' schedules. A night owl who studies with music. Doesn't mean to be disruptive — genuinely unaware of the impact. Gets defensive when criticized.
other_party.objective: Keep his routine of studying with background music. Feels the room is equally his. Doesn't want to be told what to do.
other_party.batna: Use headphones (but he finds them uncomfortable for long sessions). Or request a room change (but that's complicated and he likes the current room).
other_party.cultural_notes: Karthik responds badly to accusations but well to 'I feel' statements. He's generous — if you ask nicely, he'll help. He hates being patronized.
other_party.conversation_style: Casual, jokes to defuse tension, gets defensive when feeling attacked

scoring_criteria.relationship: Did you preserve the friendship and room dynamic?
scoring_criteria.win_win: Did you find a sustainable quiet-hours arrangement?
scoring_criteria.communication: Did you use 'I' statements instead of 'You always...'?
scoring_criteria.batna_usage: Did you explore creative solutions before escalating?

coaching_tips: DON'T start with complaints — open with something positive about living together
Use 'I feel...' instead of 'You always...' — avoid blame language
Acknowledge that the room is equally his — don't be controlling
Suggest specific, actionable compromises (quiet hours, headphones, study timings)
If he gets defensive, pause and acknowledge his feelings before continuing
learning_objectives: Practice conflict resolution with peers
Learn to use non-violent communication techniques
Develop empathy and boundary-setting skills simultaneously

storybook_pages.title: Another Sleepless Night
storybook_pages.text: 1:47 AM. Karthik's speaker is pumping EDM while he codes. Your thermodynamics exam is at 9 AM. You've been staring at the ceiling for two hours, pillow over your ears. This is the fourth night in a row.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian college hostel room at night, one student trying to sleep with pillow over ears looking frustrated, roommate at desk with headphones around neck and speaker playing music while coding, dim room with desk lamp, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Building Frustration
storybook_pages.text: The passive-aggressive sticky note you left didn't work. Neither did the loud sigh at 2 AM. You're exhausted, irritable, and your friendship is fraying. Your classmates say 'just complain to the warden.' But that feels like betrayal.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian college hostel hallway, tired frustrated student walking with dark circles under eyes, friends giving advice in the background, sticky note visible on a door, exam preparation stress visible, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Time for the Real Talk
storybook_pages.text: It's 7 PM. Karthik just got back from the mess, in a good mood. Your exam is tomorrow. If you don't talk now, you'll either explode or fail. Deep breath. 'Karthik, got a minute? I want to talk about something.'
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Indian college hostel room in the evening, two roommates facing each other, one sitting on bed looking serious but calm, the other just arrived looking surprised, room with two beds two desks books and posters, illustration style

scenarios.title: Customer Interview — Vikram, the IT Engineer
scenarios.description: You're Priya, 6 months after saving the chai stall. You want to add ONE new menu item. First conversation: Vikram, a 28-year-old IT engineer who used to be a regular but stopped buying breakfast. Listen for what he ACTUALLY needs — don't just sell him cold brew.
scenarios.setting: Outside Vikram's office building, 9:15 AM on a Tuesday
scenarios.cultural_context: Bangalore IT corridor — most engineers skip breakfast because they're rushing to morning standups. Their stated reason ('I'm just not a breakfast person') usually hides a real reason ('I don't have 10 minutes to sit down').
scenarios.your_objective: Find out what Vikram REALLY needs in the morning. Use open questions. Avoid pitching any menu item until you've heard him fully. Resist the urge to jump to 'try our cold brew!' on turn 1.
scenarios.your_batna: Walk away with surface-level info ('Vikram doesn't eat breakfast') and guess at a menu item. You'll be wrong.

other_party.name: Vikram
other_party.occupation: Software engineer at a mid-sized startup, 28
other_party.personality: Polite, in a hurry, slightly impatient with small talk. Will give one-word answers if questions are closed. Opens up when asked specific 'what was the last time you...' questions. Hates being sold to.
other_party.objective: Get a quick energy hit before his 9:30 standup. He doesn't actually want breakfast — he wants caffeine + sugar fast.
other_party.batna: Buy a bottled energy drink from the convenience store on the way in.
other_party.cultural_notes: Vikram trusts the chai stall but feels bad refusing food. Hint signals: he says 'breakfast' but means 'energy'. He says 'no time' but really means 'no time to SIT'. The right product solves the energy + portability problem.
other_party.conversation_style: Brief, professional, warms up with curiosity-based questions

scoring_criteria.listened: Did you ask open questions instead of yes/no questions?
scoring_criteria.didnt_sell: Did you AVOID pitching a menu item before turn 4?
scoring_criteria.paraphrased: Did you reflect back what Vikram said in your own words at least once?
scoring_criteria.found_real_need: Did you identify that Vikram's real need is portable morning energy, not 'breakfast'?

coaching_tips: DON'T open with 'try our new cold brew!' — open with curiosity
Ask 'what's your morning routine been like lately?' instead of 'do you eat breakfast?'
When Vikram says something interesting, paraphrase it: 'so it sounds like the issue isn't food, it's time?'
Wait until turn 4 or 5 before suggesting any product
Listen for words like 'rush', 'standup', 'no time' — those are signals about portability, not food
learning_objectives: Practice asking open vs closed questions
Practice paraphrasing — the highest-value listening move
Learn that customers describe symptoms, founders have to find needs

storybook_pages.title: The Tea Stall, Six Months Later
storybook_pages.text: The cart is back to 90% of its old numbers. Anjali brings her cousins. Krishna Mama sends a WhatsApp every time anything in the supply changes. Now you want to grow — add ONE new menu item. But which one? You decide to do what every smart founder does: ask the customers themselves.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: A small Indian chai cart in a Bangalore tech-park gully, late morning, four customers around the cart, the young woman owner looking thoughtful with a small notebook in hand, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Catching Vikram
storybook_pages.text: Vikram used to come every morning. The last 3 weeks — nothing. You spot him walking briskly toward his office building, laptop bag bouncing on his shoulder, AirPods in. He sees you, pulls one out: 'Hey Priya. Can't stop today, standup at 9:30.' This is your chance — not to sell, but to listen.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: An IT engineer in a hurry on a Bangalore tech park sidewalk, laptop bag, holding a phone, brief eye contact with a chai stall owner, mid-morning, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Rule
storybook_pages.text: You promised yourself ONE rule before this experiment: don't pitch. Just listen. The first founder instinct is to talk. Resist it. Whatever Vikram tells you, ASK ONE MORE QUESTION before you reach for the menu.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: A close-up of a small notebook with a single underlined sentence 'JUST LISTEN', pen resting on it, illustration style

scenarios.title: Customer Interview — Lakshmi Auntie
scenarios.description: Lakshmi Auntie, 58, walks her dog past your stall every evening. She used to buy chai twice a week. Lately, never. She'll give you 5 minutes — but she won't say what's actually wrong unless you make her feel heard.
scenarios.setting: Park bench at sunset, with Lakshmi's small dog at her feet
scenarios.cultural_context: Older customers often say 'too sweet' when they mean 'I'm watching my health' — but they don't say the second part because it feels like complaining. They want to be asked, not sold to. Respect for elders matters; rushing the conversation is rude.
scenarios.your_objective: Find out why Lakshmi stopped coming. Listen for the real reason underneath 'everything is too sweet now'. Don't jump to suggesting oat-milk chai — discover whether sweetness, sugar, or tradition is the real lever.
scenarios.your_batna: Take her surface complaint at face value, reduce sugar by 20%, and lose her anyway because the issue isn't really sweetness — it's nostalgia for how chai used to taste 30 years ago.

other_party.name: Lakshmi Auntie
other_party.occupation: Retired schoolteacher, 58, lives alone with her dog
other_party.personality: Warm, observant, slightly wary of being sold to. Has strong opinions but masks them with politeness. Will say 'oh, it's nothing' and then mention something specific. Watch for the second sentence after the deflection.
other_party.objective: Have someone listen to her actually. Underneath, she wants chai that doesn't spike her blood sugar — but she's embarrassed to mention diabetes risk to a young chai-stall owner.
other_party.batna: Make chai at home with stevia. Tastes wrong but at least it's safe.
other_party.cultural_notes: Lakshmi will warm up if you ask about her late mother or her dog. She uses the phrase 'these days' to mean 'I'm getting older'. She trusts people who notice details about her without asking.
other_party.conversation_style: Polite deflection followed by very specific honesty when the listener earns it

scoring_criteria.patience: Did you wait through the deflection ('oh, it's nothing') for the real answer?
scoring_criteria.respectful: Did you avoid arguing with her stated reason?
scoring_criteria.found_real_need: Did you identify health/sugar as the underlying need, NOT just sweetness?
scoring_criteria.personal_warmth: Did you ask about her, not just her chai habits?

coaching_tips: DO start with something personal — ask about her dog or how her week has been
When she says 'oh, it's nothing important', stay quiet — she'll often follow up with the real thing
If she says 'too sweet', DON'T jump to 'we can reduce sugar!' — ask 'has anything else changed?'
Don't dismiss tradition — many older customers want chai that tastes 'like before', not modernised
Notice if she mentions health, doctor visits, or her late husband/mother — those are gold
learning_objectives: Practice patience in conversations — the second answer is usually the real one
Learn that older customers often disguise health concerns as taste complaints
Practice respecting cultural deflection without ignoring the real signal

storybook_pages.title: The Evening Walk
storybook_pages.text: Lakshmi Auntie walks past every evening at 6 PM with her small dog. Today she stops, finally. 'Priya beta, how is your uncle?' she asks. You say he's well, then ask if she'd sit with you for a few minutes. She nods, settling on the park bench, the dog curling at her feet.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: A 58-year-old Indian woman with grey-streaked hair sitting on a park bench at golden hour, small dog at her feet, gentle smile, warm illustration style

storybook_pages.title: What She Won't Say First
storybook_pages.text: Lakshmi Auntie is the kind of person who will say 'oh nothing has changed' as a deflection — and then, if you stay quiet, will say something completely different. The trick is: don't fill the silence. Let her finish her own sentence.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Two figures on a park bench in soft evening light, a younger woman listening attentively, an older woman mid-thought, gentle warm illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Listen for the Subtext
storybook_pages.text: When she finally talks about your chai, listen for WHAT she compares it to. Her mother's chai. Her own kitchen. 'These days'. Each phrase is telling you something underneath the words.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Close-up illustration of two steel chai tumblers, one fresh and one in a worn faded photograph, soft golden light, illustration style

scenarios.title: Customer Interview — Rohit, the School Student
scenarios.description: Rohit, 16, plays football after school and stops at your stall on the way home — sometimes. He says he's 'bored of maggi' but his real need is something different. Listen carefully.
scenarios.setting: Just outside the stall at 5:45 PM, Rohit in muddy football kit
scenarios.cultural_context: Teenage Indian boys often confuse 'bored' with 'still hungry'. They use 'I want something new' to mean 'I want something more substantial'. Take their stated reason as a starting point, not a destination.
scenarios.your_objective: Find out what Rohit ACTUALLY wants after football practice. Don't get tricked by 'I'm bored of maggi' into thinking he wants novelty — he might want more food or a different macronutrient.
scenarios.your_batna: Add cold brew to the menu (because 'teens like new things') and watch Rohit ignore it because he wanted dinner-equivalent calories.

other_party.name: Rohit
other_party.occupation: Class 11 student, plays striker for the school football team
other_party.personality: Direct, slightly impatient, hungry. Will tell you exactly what he thinks if you ask the right question — but his FIRST answer is usually performative ('I'm cool, I just want something different'). His SECOND answer is honest ('I'm starving and maggi doesn't fill me up anymore').
other_party.objective: Get something fast, cheap (under ₹40), filling enough to skip dinner if his mother is late. Doesn't want to admit to being that hungry — feels uncool.
other_party.batna: Buy two packets of biscuits from the kirana store. Cheap and filling but he knows it's bad.
other_party.cultural_notes: Rohit will brag about football performance. Use that as a way in — 'how was practice?' — and watch him eat his words about being 'not that hungry' within two turns.
other_party.conversation_style: Casual, slightly performative, opens up when asked about football

scoring_criteria.didnt_take_first_answer: Did you ask follow-up questions instead of accepting 'I'm bored of maggi'?
scoring_criteria.found_real_need: Did you identify HUNGER + FILLING as the real need, not novelty?
scoring_criteria.respected_pride: Did you avoid embarrassing him about being hungry?
scoring_criteria.right_recommendation: Did you propose a heavier item (samosa-chaat or similar), not a lighter one (cold brew)?

coaching_tips: Open with football — 'how was practice today?' — and let him brag for a bit
When he says 'bored of maggi', ask 'when did you last eat?' — answer reveals truth
Watch the body language clues in his messages: tired, sweaty, leans on the cart
DON'T pitch cold brew to a hungry footballer — he'll think you didn't listen
learning_objectives: Practice listening past performative first answers
Learn that 'bored of X' often means 'X doesn't solve my real problem'
Match recommendations to real needs, not stated preferences

storybook_pages.title: The Footballer After Practice
storybook_pages.text: Rohit walks up to the stall in muddy football kit, jersey untucked, hair flattened by sweat. He drops his bag on the ground. 'Priya didi, what's new today?' His voice is casual but his hand is already reaching for the biscuit jar.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: A 16-year-old Indian boy in a sweaty muddy football kit standing at a chai stall, school bag on the ground, golden hour light, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The 'I'm Bored of Maggi' Trap
storybook_pages.text: He says he's bored of maggi. The lazy founder hears: 'he wants new'. The thoughtful founder hears: 'maggi doesn't fill him up after football, but he doesn't want to say he's that hungry.' These are completely different briefs for a menu.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: A close-up illustration of a steaming bowl of maggi noodles next to a hungrier dish like samosa-chaat, divided down the middle, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Ask the Football Question
storybook_pages.text: Two questions cut through the bravado: 'how was practice?' and 'when did you last eat?'. The first lets him brag. The second tells you the truth. The right menu item is in between those two answers.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Two thought-bubbles in cartoon style, one full of football poses, the other full of an empty stomach symbol, illustration style

scenarios.title: Customer Interview — Anjali Returns
scenarios.description: Anjali — the regular who almost left during the milk crisis — is back. She comes daily. Now you want to know: what would make her stay 5 extra minutes? What would make this stall the place she chooses on a hard day?
scenarios.setting: A quiet 4 PM at the stall, Anjali on the corner stool with her chai
scenarios.cultural_context: Loyal customers are usually under-asked — founders take them for granted. Asking a returning customer 'what would make this BETTER for you?' is a strategic move. They will tell you things new customers can't because they actually use the product.
scenarios.your_objective: Find out what would deepen Anjali's relationship with the stall — not just what she'd buy, but what would make her LINGER. Listen for emotional language, not just product preferences.
scenarios.your_batna: Don't ask, and watch Anjali's daily visit slowly become a 90-second pickup instead of a 10-minute pause in her day.

other_party.name: Anjali
other_party.occupation: 32-year-old marketing manager at an IT firm
other_party.personality: Articulate, reflective, slightly nostalgic. Recently widowed, she doesn't share that easily — but she trusts the stall. She'll tell you the whole truth if asked the right question, and clam up if pushed too hard.
other_party.objective: Find a place where she can be alone but not lonely. The stall already does this on her good days. She wants it to keep doing it on her bad days.
other_party.batna: Make tea at home alone. Sad, but predictable.
other_party.cultural_notes: Anjali responds to questions about ritual, comfort, and 'home'. She's allergic to 'value-add' marketing language. The right item to add isn't food — it's an experience: a small bench, a regular's mug, a 'no rush' policy.
other_party.conversation_style: Thoughtful, emotionally fluent when invited, defensive when not

scoring_criteria.listened_to_emotion: Did you ask emotional, not transactional, questions?
scoring_criteria.didnt_pitch_product: Did you avoid trying to upsell a new menu item to her?
scoring_criteria.found_real_need: Did you identify a ritual/experience need, not a product need?
scoring_criteria.preserved_dignity: Did you respect her dignity — never asking 'why are you sad' directly?

coaching_tips: Open with gratitude: 'I want to thank you for coming back after that whole milk thing'
Ask 'what makes a really good chai-stop for you, on a tough day?' — emotional, not transactional
Listen for words like 'home', 'breath', 'pause', 'mum' — those are ritual signals
Resist pitching samosas. The right answer for Anjali might be 'add a corner bench' — not a menu item
End by repeating back what you heard, exactly in her words. Don't paraphrase to commercial language.
learning_objectives: Practice emotional, not transactional, customer interviews
Learn that the best 'product addition' is sometimes an experience, not an item
Practice respecting dignity in vulnerable conversations

storybook_pages.title: Anjali on the Stool
storybook_pages.text: She's been coming back daily since the milk story resolved. Always between 4 and 4:30 PM. Always the corner stool. She drinks her chai slowly. Sometimes she stays 10 minutes. Sometimes 30. You realise — you've never asked her why this place. Just why she stopped coming. Time to ask the better question.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: A 32-year-old Indian woman sitting on a corner stool at a chai stall, holding a steel tumbler with both hands, late afternoon golden light, contemplative expression, illustration style

storybook_pages.title: The Question Most Founders Don't Ask
storybook_pages.text: 'What makes a place feel like a place you want to come back to?' — that question is bigger than 'what should I add to the menu?'. It tells you whether your customer is buying chai, or buying something chai represents.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: Two thought bubbles, one with a steaming cup of chai, one with a memory of a small kitchen and a mother, soft illustration style

storybook_pages.title: Don't Convert It Into a Product
storybook_pages.text: When Anjali tells you she comes here to breathe — RESIST converting that into 'aha! she'd love our breathwork-themed chai!'. The right answer might be silence. A bench. A mug with her name on it. Don't sell where you should serve.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: A small wooden corner bench at a chai stall with a single steel tumbler resting on it, late afternoon shadow, no people, illustration style

transfer_exercises.game_context: Managing resources across multiple rounds to reach the best outcome
transfer_exercises.real_world: Planning study time over a semester rather than cramming before exams
transfer_exercises.challenge: Create a resource management plan for your next month: budget time/money/energy across competing priorities.

transfer_exercises.game_context: Recovering from negative events across game rounds
transfer_exercises.real_world: Maintaining performance after setbacks in a sports season or project
transfer_exercises.challenge: Track your energy/mood for 5 days. Notice patterns. What depletes you? What restores you?

glossary_terms.definition: The process of selecting among alternatives based on available information and values.
glossary_terms.example: Choosing between two career paths based on income, passion, and long-term growth.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Good decision-making combines rational analysis with awareness of cognitive biases that distort judgment.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Leaders make high-stakes decisions daily — the quality of their process matters as much as the decision itself.

glossary_terms.definition: Analyzing information objectively to form a well-reasoned judgment.
glossary_terms.example: Questioning whether a statistic is representative before using it to make a decision.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Critical thinking involves identifying assumptions, evaluating evidence, and considering alternative perspectives.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Journalists fact-check before publishing; scientists replicate experiments before claiming discoveries.

glossary_terms.definition: The belief that abilities can be developed through effort and learning from failure.
glossary_terms.example: Seeing a poor game result as feedback on what to practice, not evidence of being bad at the game.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Research by Carol Dweck shows people with growth mindsets achieve more and recover better from setbacks.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Students who believe intelligence is fixed give up when challenged; those with growth mindset persist and improve.

title: Negotiation Arena
description: Enter a live negotiation scenario where both sides have hidden interests and limited time. Develop the strategies, listening skills, and creative thinking that great negotiators use.
coaching_moment: Enter a live negotiation scenario where both sides have hidden interests and limited time. Develop the strategies, listening skills, and creative thinking that great negotiators use.
cultural_context: Negotiation is central to Indian professional and business culture — from vendor relationships to corporate deal-making to daily commerce. Learning principled negotiation (interests vs positions) is a high-leverage skill for Indian professionals at every stage of their career.
learning_objectives: Develop critical thinking through negotiation gameplay
Practice decision-making in realistic scenarios
Build self-awareness about your strengths and areas for growth
reflection_prompt: Where did you give ground, and where did you hold it? What did the other side teach you about your own priorities?
